meta.name: ISC2 Systems Security Certified Practitioner (SSCP)
meta.notes: Initial pack — 12 questions across the 7 SSCP domains (scheduled-agent).

questions.question: A junior admin discovers she has been assigned to both the Application Developers group and the Change Approvers group, giving her the ability to write code and sign off on her own production releases. Which security principle does this arrangement violate?
options: Separation of duties — a single person can execute and authorize a high-risk workflow end-to-end
Defense in depth — controls are layered inefficiently across too many groups
Non-repudiation — the developer can later deny writing the code that was approved
Data classification — released code is not labelled with a sensitivity level
questions.explanation: Separation of duties (SoD) requires that critical activities such as writing and approving a change be split across two individuals so no one person can commit fraud or push malicious code unchecked. Defense in depth is about layered controls (firewall + IDS + endpoint), not who performs each task. Non-repudiation prevents users from denying past actions and is enforced by logging and digital signatures, not by role assignment. Data classification labels information sensitivity and is unrelated to who can approve a code change.

questions.question: A firewall administrator is instructed to only allow inbound HTTPS to the web tier and to deny everything else, including protocols nobody has asked for. Which default posture is being applied?
options: Implicit allow — traffic is permitted unless explicitly blocked
Fail-open — a failed rule evaluation lets traffic through
Implicit deny — traffic is blocked unless explicitly permitted
Round-robin — connections are distributed across matching rules
questions.explanation: Implicit deny is the industry-standard baseline: any traffic not matched by an explicit allow rule is dropped. Implicit allow is the opposite posture and is considered insecure because it forces admins to enumerate every unwanted protocol. Fail-open describes the behaviour of a broken control that stops enforcing rules (a resilience choice, not a default posture). Round-robin is a load-balancing algorithm and has nothing to do with rule evaluation defaults.

questions.question: An organization is choosing an access-control model where permissions are attached to positions such as `Nurse`, `Pharmacist`, or `Billing Clerk`, and users inherit those permissions when assigned to a position. Which model best fits this description?
options: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) — resource owners grant permissions directly to individuals
Mandatory Access Control (MAC) — access decisions are based on labels and clearances set by policy
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) — permissions are bundled into roles that users are assigned
Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) — decisions are computed from user, resource, and context attributes
questions.explanation: RBAC bundles permissions into roles (job functions) and grants users access indirectly by assigning them the role — exactly the described `Nurse`, `Pharmacist`, `Billing Clerk` pattern. DAC leaves the grant decision to the resource owner (typical file-system ACLs). MAC forces decisions from a security label / clearance policy the user cannot override (typical of Bell-LaPadula / Biba systems). ABAC composes rules from arbitrary user, resource, and environmental attributes (department, time-of-day, device posture) rather than pre-built roles.

questions.question: During a quantitative risk assessment, an analyst calculates SLE = $50,000 and ARO = 0.2. What is the Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) for this risk?
options: $5,000 — SLE divided by ARO
$10,000 — SLE multiplied by ARO
$50,200 — SLE plus ARO
$250,000 — SLE divided by ARO expressed as a percentage
questions.explanation: ALE = SLE × ARO by definition. $50,000 × 0.2 = $10,000, meaning the organization expects to lose $10,000 per year on average from this risk. Dividing SLE by ARO or adding them are common trap answers that mis-apply the formula; the $250,000 figure comes from mis-reading ARO 0.2 as a 20% discount factor. ALE is the value compared to the annual cost of a proposed safeguard when deciding whether to accept, mitigate, or transfer a risk.

questions.question: An analyst needs to detect a previously unseen ransomware variant that has no published signature. Which detection approach is most likely to catch it?
options: Signature-based detection — match traffic against a known malware pattern database
Anomaly / behavior-based detection — flag deviations from an established baseline of normal activity
Allow-list filtering — block anything not on an approved list of source IPs
Port-based classification — infer application identity from the destination port
questions.explanation: Signature-based tools cannot match a variant whose signature does not yet exist, so novel or zero-day malware routinely slips past them. Anomaly / behavior-based detection builds a baseline of normal process, file, and network behaviour and alerts on statistically significant deviations (e.g., a file server suddenly reading and re-writing thousands of documents), which is the classic signal for previously unseen ransomware. IP allow-lists only restrict source addresses and would not detect malicious behaviour from an already-permitted host. Port-based classification is easily evaded and does not detect malicious intent at all.

questions.question: During incident response, a first responder unplugs a compromised laptop from the network but leaves it powered on and preserves memory before shutting down. Which incident-response phase is she performing?
options: Preparation — establishing tools and playbooks before an incident occurs
Detection and analysis — determining that an incident has actually occurred
Containment — limiting the scope and impact while preserving evidence for later analysis
Lessons learned — improving controls and playbooks after the incident is closed
questions.explanation: Containment isolates the affected system to prevent further damage or lateral movement while intentionally preserving volatile evidence such as RAM contents, active network sessions, and running processes for forensic analysis — exactly what the responder is doing. Preparation is the pre-incident work of writing playbooks and provisioning tooling. Detection and analysis is the earlier phase that concluded the laptop was in fact compromised. Lessons learned is the closing phase, run after eradication and recovery, focused on updating controls and documentation.

questions.question: A backup strategy runs a full backup every Sunday and captures only the blocks that changed since the previous night's backup Monday through Saturday. To restore Friday's state, how many backup sets must be applied?
options: Only the most recent full backup — differential backups are self-contained
The Sunday full backup plus every incremental backup from Monday through Friday
The Sunday full backup plus Friday's differential backup only
The Sunday full backup plus Wednesday's mid-week checkpoint
questions.explanation: The scenario describes incremental backups: each nightly job captures only what changed since the previous backup. A restore therefore requires the last full backup (Sunday) plus every incremental in sequence up to the target day (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday). Differential backups, by contrast, capture everything changed since the last full backup, so a differential restore would need only the full plus the most recent differential — but that is not what the scenario says. There is no `mid-week checkpoint` in the described strategy.

questions.question: A developer wants to protect passwords in a database so that two users choosing the same password produce different stored values and offline brute-force is expensive per guess. Which technique satisfies BOTH requirements?
options: Store a raw SHA-256 hash of each password
Encrypt each password with AES-256 using a shared server key
Store a per-user random salt and apply a slow key-derivation function such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
Store passwords in plaintext inside a database with column-level encryption at rest
questions.explanation: A per-user random salt guarantees that identical passwords hash to different stored values and defeats precomputed rainbow tables. A deliberately slow key-derivation function (bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2) forces the attacker to spend meaningful CPU / memory per guess, which is what makes offline brute-force impractical. Raw SHA-256 is fast and unsalted, so identical passwords collide and modern GPUs can try billions per second. AES with a shared key is reversible — anyone who steals the key recovers every password. Column-level encryption at rest still leaves the plaintext visible to the application and does nothing against a compromised DB backup.

questions.question: Two parties who have never met need to establish a shared symmetric session key across an untrusted network without ever transmitting the key itself. Which cryptographic mechanism is designed for this?
options: AES-256 in CBC mode — a symmetric block cipher used with a pre-shared key
SHA-3 — a hashing algorithm that produces a fixed-length digest
Diffie-Hellman key exchange — an asymmetric protocol that lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel
HMAC — a keyed hash construction used for message authentication
questions.explanation: Diffie-Hellman (and its elliptic-curve variant ECDH) is specifically designed so two parties can compute the same shared secret by exchanging only public values, without ever transmitting the secret itself — the foundational primitive for TLS key agreement. AES is the symmetric cipher used AFTER the key is agreed, and it assumes the key is already shared. SHA-3 is a one-way hash and cannot establish a key. HMAC uses an already-shared secret to authenticate messages; it does not create the shared secret in the first place.

questions.question: A retail chain wants an isolated network segment for point-of-sale terminals so that a compromise of the corporate LAN cannot pivot into the PCI cardholder-data environment. Which network-security technique most directly implements this goal?
options: Traffic shaping — prioritize latency-sensitive protocols on the shared link
Network segmentation with a firewall / VLAN between zones of differing trust levels
Port Address Translation (PAT) — hide many internal addresses behind one public IP
Split-horizon DNS — return different address records to internal vs external clients
questions.explanation: Segmenting the POS environment into its own zone with a firewall or ACL-enforced VLAN boundary limits blast radius: an attacker who lands in the corporate LAN still has to defeat the segmentation control before touching cardholder data. This is exactly the intent of the PCI DSS scoping requirement. Traffic shaping is a QoS technique with no security benefit. PAT hides addresses but does not restrict which zones can talk to each other. Split-horizon DNS just changes which records are returned by view; it does not enforce traffic isolation.

questions.question: A hypervisor hosts several tenant VMs on the same physical host. Which risk is UNIQUE to virtualized environments and would not exist on stand-alone physical servers?
options: Unpatched operating systems in the guest VMs
VM escape — a guest exploits the hypervisor to reach the host or other tenant VMs
Weak administrator passwords on network devices
Employees plugging in unauthorized USB drives
questions.explanation: VM escape is the class of vulnerability where malicious code inside a guest breaks out of its virtual machine and gains code execution on the hypervisor or on a neighbouring tenant. It exists only because a hypervisor is sharing hardware between tenants — a stand-alone physical server has no such shared boundary to defeat. Unpatched OSes, weak admin passwords, and rogue USB drives are all real risks but are just as present on physical hardware, so they are not unique to virtualization.

questions.question: A web application accepts a user-supplied filename and reads it from disk using `open('/var/data/' + filename)`. A researcher shows that requesting `../../etc/passwd` returns the contents of the host's password file. What class of vulnerability is this?
options: SQL injection — attacker-supplied input alters a database query
Cross-site scripting (XSS) — attacker-supplied input is reflected into another user's browser
Path traversal (directory traversal) — attacker-supplied input escapes the intended directory using relative path segments
Server-side request forgery (SSRF) — the server is coerced into making an unintended outbound request
questions.explanation: The attacker is escaping the intended `/var/data/` directory by including `..` segments so the operating system resolves the path to a location the app never meant to expose — the textbook definition of a path-traversal (a.k.a. directory-traversal) flaw, catalogued as CWE-22. SQL injection targets database queries, not filesystem paths. XSS abuses HTML/JS rendering in a victim's browser. SSRF tricks the server into making outbound network requests. The fix is to canonicalise the path and reject any result that leaves the allow-listed base directory.
